title: Running backs as receivers: the swing, the angle, the wheel and the checkdown (and why McCaffrey had 161 receiving yards)
html:
Why this lesson now: the Film Room mirror (football-brief, branch film-room) was checked this run. It still holds one logged game file (data/games/gmum7mktl1wy3.json, "Eagles at Bears, Week 3", no snaps logged) and no review files. The backup source (football-film-room, branch "data") couldn't be read: "repository foolserrandsf/football-film-room is not configured for this session." So there's no new miss of yours to fix, and no snap of yours this connects to yet. It's a new concept from Sunday, when running backs caught passes for big yards all over the league.

The big idea: a running back doesn't only take handoffs. On pass plays he's often a receiver too.He starts in the backfield, so the defense usually covers him with a linebacker (LB). Linebackers are built to stop runs, and many are slower than a good back.That mismatch is why backs can pile up receiving yards.

Labels A–D match the routes below. Solid lines are quick routes; the dashed line (C) goes deep. LB = linebacker.

  1. A · The swing. The back arcs out toward the sideline, behind the line. It's a long handoff: catch it in space and run.Sunday: Carolina's Chuba Hubbard caught 5 passes for 80 yards to go with 92 rushing yards and 2 TDs (ESPN).
  2. B · The angle. The back starts outside like a swing, then cuts hard back inside.The linebacker chasing him outside can't stop and turn fast enough. It beats man coverage (Lesson 5).
  3. C · The wheel. He runs to the flat, then turns straight up the sideline.If a linebacker has to follow him 30 yards downfield, it's usually a big play.Sunday: Christian McCaffrey caught TDs of 74 and 66 yards and had 161 receiving yards, his career best (FOX Sports).
  4. D · The checkdown. The back slips past the line and sits in an open spot in the middle.It's the QB's safety valve when the receivers are covered. Short gain, but no sack (Lesson 55).Sunday: Jahmyr Gibbs caught 7 passes for 99 yards and ran for 153 more in Munich. Rookie Emmett Johnson had 6 catches for 70 yards and 2 TDs in his first Chiefs start.

Why it matters for bets: a back's catches don't count toward his rushing-yards prop. Gordon's 76 rushing yards were his bet; the rest of his 115 scrimmage yards were catches.When a team is behind, its back catches more and runs less (Lesson 51). That can sink a rushing prop but help a receiving one.Tonight: if the Chargers fall behind, Omarion Hampton's catches matter more than his 34.5 rushing yards.

For your Film Room drill: look at where the back lines up before the snap.Directly behind the QB: run is more likely. Beside the QB (offset) with the QB in shotgun: either one.Split out wide, or no back at all (an "empty" backfield): guess pass.

Connecting the dots: Lesson 37 showed the screen, a planned throw to the back behind the line. Lesson 52 drew the route tree for receivers. These are the back's own routes, and Lesson 49's hot route is often one of them.

Video: search YouTube for "running back wheel route explained" and "Christian McCaffrey 74 yard touchdown Cowboys."

Practice it in Football Camp → (Station 5: Plays)

quiz.q: Which route has the running back go to the flat, then turn straight up the sideline?
quiz.w: The wheel (C). It's dangerous because a linebacker has to chase the back deep.

quiz.q: Why is a running back often open as a receiver?
o: A linebacker usually covers him, and many are slower than the back
He's allowed to start past the line
Backs can't be tackled after a catch
quiz.w: Linebackers are built to stop runs. In space, a quick back can beat them.

quiz.q: Before the snap, the offense has no back in the backfield (empty). What should you guess in your drill?
quiz.w: With no back behind the QB, there's no one to hand it to. Empty almost always means pass.

quiz.q: Ollie Gordon II had 76 rushing yards and 115 scrimmage yards. What counts for a "60+ rushing yards" bet?
quiz.w: Only rushing yards count. His catches (the other 39 scrimmage yards) don't.
